hints: Notice the question asks for the pair that must increase density for any size of change, so start from $\rho = m/V$.
Think how density responds when the numerator $m$ gets larger and separately how it responds when the denominator $V$ gets smaller.
Check each row of the mass-volume table to see if both changes push $m/V$ upward or if they oppose each other.
walkthrough: Recall the definition of density: $\rho = m/V$, where $m$ is mass and $V$ is volume.
Density increases if the numerator increases with $V$ fixed, because more mass is packed into the same volume.
Density also increases if the denominator decreases with $m$ fixed, because the same mass is packed into less volume.
Combining both effects, increasing $m$ while decreasing $V$ makes the fraction $m/V$ larger in both ways, so the increase is guaranteed.
The other pairs either both push density the same uncertain way or push in opposite directions, so the result depends on the amounts changed. This is option C

options.A: Both numerator and denominator of $\rho = m/V$ get smaller, so the ratio could increase, decrease or stay the same depending on the relative sizes of the changes.
options.B: A smaller mass divided by a larger volume gives a smaller value of $m/V$, so density must decrease.
options.C: A larger mass divided by a smaller volume gives a larger value of $m/V$, so density must increase.
options.D: Both mass and volume get larger, so the ratio $m/V$ could increase, decrease or stay the same depending on which change is proportionally larger.
